Heat welding fuses materials like plastics or flooring using heat and a filler rod to create a seamless bond.

The Process

  1. Clean and Prep: Groove the seam where the two pieces meet using a hand groover or router to create a "V" or "U" shape.
  2. Set the Temperature: Heat your welding gun to the specific melting point of your material (typically 200°C to 450°C).
  3. Apply Filler: Insert a matching welding rod into the high-speed nozzle.
  4. Weld: Move the gun steadily along the groove, allowing the heat to melt both the rod and the base material into a single pool.
  5. Trim: While the weld is still warm, use a Mozart knife or spatula knife with a trim guide to cut away the excess rod flush with the surface.

turns.prompt_text: can you show me a few examples of welding rods used for steel or aluminum
turns.response_html:
Welding rods vary by metal type, thickness, and the specific welding process (Stick or TIG).

Steel Welding Rods (Stick/SMAW)

  • 6010: Deep penetration for dirty or rusted metal; used often in pipe welding.
  • 6011: Similar to 6010 but works with both AC and DC welders.
  • 6013: Provides a smooth arc and easy slag removal; great for beginners or sheet metal.
  • 7018: High-strength rod for structural steel; requires a dry storage environment.

Aluminum Welding Rods (TIG/GTAW or Stick)

  • 4043: Contains silicon; flows easily and is highly resistant to cracking. Common for general repair.
  • 5356: Contains magnesium; stronger and stiffer than 4043. Best for marine environments or anodized finishes.

Crucial Note: Never use a steel rod on aluminum or vice versa, as they will not bond and will contaminate your weld pool.
